lesson.title: One Estimate to Test Them: The Pooled Proportion
lesson.summary: When a hypothesis test assumes two population proportions are equal, the pooled proportion combines both samples into a single shared estimate, giving a more appropriate standard error than treating the groups separately.
lesson.body:
The confidence interval for a difference in proportions, built in the previous chapter, deliberately keeps the two groups' variability separate, because a confidence interval makes no assumption that p1 equals p2, it is trying to estimate whatever that difference actually is. Hypothesis testing, covered in the chapters ahead, works differently: a test of whether two proportions are equal starts by assuming, for the sake of argument, that the null hypothesis p1 equals p2 is true. If that assumption holds, then both samples are not estimating two different quantities at all, they are two independent estimates of one single, shared population proportion. It makes sense, in that situation, to combine the data from both groups into one pooled estimate rather than keeping them apart.

The pooled proportion is defined as p-hat pooled equals (x1 plus x2) divided by (n1 plus n2), where x1 and x2 are the counts of successes in each sample and n1 and n2 are the two sample sizes. It is exactly what you would get by mentally combining both samples into one large sample and computing an ordinary sample proportion. Once you have p-hat pooled, the standard error used under the null hypothesis is the square root of p-hat pooled times (1 minus p-hat pooled) times (1/n1 plus 1/n2).

Worked example, reusing the tutoring program data from the previous chapter: Program A had x1 = 175 successes out of n1 = 250, and Program B had x2 = 150 successes out of n2 = 250. The pooled proportion is (175 plus 150) divided by (250 plus 250), which is 325/500 = 0.65. The pooled standard error is the square root of 0.65 times 0.35 times (1/250 plus 1/250), which is the square root of 0.2275 times 0.008, or the square root of 0.00182, about 0.0427.

Compare that to the unpooled standard error from the confidence interval chapter, about 0.0424, close but not identical. The two numbers differ because the pooled version forces a single shared variance estimate built from the combined 0.65 proportion, while the unpooled version lets each group's own proportion, 0.70 and 0.60, drive its own contribution to the variability. That distinction matters: use the pooled proportion specifically when testing the hypothesis that p1 equals p2, and use the separate, unpooled standard error when building a confidence interval for the difference, since a confidence interval is not assuming the groups are equal in the first place. With this tool in hand, the next chapters turn fully to how hypothesis tests are structured, starting from the ground up.
